title: Burns: assessment and fluid resuscitation
subject: surgery
summary: Airway first, then measure the burn, calculate fluids and steer them by urine output.

objectives.text: Pick the first step in a burn patient and decide when to intubate before oedema closes the airway
Choose the test that confirms inhalation injury and reject pulse oximetry, chest X-ray and ABG as reassurance or proof
Pair the antidote or treatment with the poison: CO, cyanide, hydrofluoric acid
Name the type of burn shock and choose the resuscitation fluid, with and without colloid
Grade burn depth from pain, blanching and appearance, and decide what counts toward TBSA
Estimate TBSA with the correct rule of nines values, switching to child figures when the patient is a child
Calculate the Parkland volume, time the first half from the burn, and deduct fluid already given
Titrate fluid hourly to the right urine output target for age and setting, and read over- versus under-resuscitation
Pair each topical agent with its side effect or property
Tell Curling's ulcer from Marjolin's ulcer and place each in the burn timeline

traps.trap: Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA is the answer to every fluid question
The 8-hour half of the Parkland volume is counted from arrival at hospital
Halving the 24-hour total in the wrong place (whole 24 h volume given in 8 h, or half given over 24 h)
Volume already given before arrival is not deducted from the first-8-hour total
The adult rule of nines is applied to a child
Colloid is given in the first 24 h of classic Parkland, or Parkland is confused with Evans and Brooke
A chest X-ray or arterial blood gas is taken as the test that confirms inhalation injury
Pulse oximetry is used as reassurance that carbon monoxide poisoning is excluded
Curling's ulcer and Marjolin's ulcer are swapped
The formula is followed rigidly, with no hourly titration to urine output
Fluid is increased when urine output is high, and reduced when it is low
Pain tracks depth in a straight line, so the least painful burn is taken as full thickness
The adult urine output target (0.5 mL/kg/h) is used in a child, and kept in special settings such as electrical injury
Rule-of-nines values are swapped, for example perineum or head given the wrong figure
Escharotomy is offered for any deep or any circumferential burn, or without the full-thickness qualifier
Topical agents are paired with the wrong side effect or the wrong property (including eschar penetration)
Antidotes are paired with the wrong poison (CO versus cyanide)
Burn assessment and fluid calculation start before the primary survey
Intubation is delayed until oedema or obstruction is established
Burn shock is called septic or cardiogenic instead of hypovolaemic

Not sure, give me a hint

Hyperbaric oxygen, the strongest form of oxygen therapy
Not sure, give me a hint

A 40-year-old has a 35% scald to the chest and both legs, seen 6 hours after the burn.
BP 85/50, pulse 130, urine 15 mL/h. Haematocrit has risen from 42 to 55. Temperature 37.2 °C. What type of shock is this?

choices.label: Septic shock, from the infected burn
Cardiogenic shock, from a failing pump
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what has left the circulation. Haematocrit rises when plasma leaves the vessels, and urine falls with it.
That is not right. Infection is a later threat, not the first cause of shock in the opening hours.
Look at the haematocrit. Which way is it moving, and what does that say is leaving the blood?
Septic shock tempts because burns do get infected, and sepsis is a real killer after the first 48 to 72 hours.
But early burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic: capillary leak moves plasma out, haematocrit rises and urine falls. Heart depression is an add-on.
That is not right. A weak pump is only a secondary factor in early burn shock.
Check the blood count and the urine. What do they say about the volume that is missing?
Cardiogenic shock tempts because the burn does depress myocardial function, and that part is real.
But the main problem is plasma loss: haematocrit rises and urine falls, so volume comes first.
Yes. A rising haematocrit and low urine output both mean plasma is leaving the circulation.
Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, with some myocardial depression from mediators.

choices.label: Why does plasma leak so fast?

say.text: A local burn releases histamine, prostaglandins and free radicals, which make the capillaries leaky.
The leak starts within minutes, peaks at 8 to 12 hours and runs on for up to 24 hours.
Still in the first 24 hours. The heart is a little depressed. What is the first-line treatment for this shock?

choices.label: Inotropes to support the failing heart
Albumin infusion at full dose from the start
Ringer lactate titrated to urine output
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the body is short of. The missing part is plasma volume, and it is the volume that goes back first.
That is not right. Inotropes treat a weak heart, and the heart is not the main problem in burn shock.
What is missing from the circulation? Think about the haematocrit and the urine again.
That is not right. Albumin has a role in burn care, but it is not the first fluid at the start.
Check the timing. What does classic practice give in the first hours, and when does colloid come in?
Albumin tempts because burns do lose protein, and albumin is a familiar fluid on the ward.
But the leak is the first problem, and classic Parkland gives crystalloid alone in the first 24 hours. Colloid comes later, about 8 to 24 hours, or when needs are very high.
Yes. Ringer lactate is the fluid of choice, and it is titrated to urine output rather than fixed.
Large volumes of saline cause hyperchloraemic acidosis, which is why Ringer lactate is preferred.
In classic Parkland the first 24 hours are crystalloid only. Evans and Brooke carry colloid, with dextrose in water.
A forearm burn, mottled red and white. It hurts less than the skin around it, and it refills slowly when pressed.
What depth is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Grade the burn by the skin first: its colour, whether it blanches, and how it refills. Then ask whether the pain agrees.
That is not right. Less painful is not the same as painless, and this burn is not insensate.
Look at the sensation in the stem again. Is the forearm insensate, or only less painful?
Full thickness tempts because a burn that has lost feeling sounds like the worst burn, and reduced pain seems to tell the same story.
Deep partial is less painful, mottled and slow to refill. Full thickness is painless, dry, leathery and does not blanch.
That is not right. Superficial partial burns are blistered, moist, pink and very painful, and they blanch.
Less pain can look like a shallower step, but this burn is mottled with sluggish refill. Which depth has those signs?
Yes. Mottled, less painful and slow to refill fits deep partial thickness. Less pain is a clue to deep injury, not to full thickness.
Depth is read by pain, blanching and appearance together. Underestimating depth is the commonest error.
Simple erythema is not counted toward the burn area for resuscitation.
Which feature separates full thickness from deep partial thickness?

choices.label: Less painful than the skin around it
Painless, dry, leathery, does not blanch
Healing takes over 3 weeks, with scarring
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with sensation. Which description says the feeling is gone, and which only says the burn hurts less?
That is not right. Deep partial burns also hurt less than normal skin, so reduced pain does not separate the two.
Pain is the first thing you check at the bedside, so it feels like the separator. Ask whether sensation is gone, not whether it hurts less.
That is not right. Slow healing with scarring describes deep partial burns, so it cannot separate the two.
Duration is a favourite exam clue, but on the day you judge sensation, blanching and dryness. Depth often declares itself only at 48 to 72 hours.
Yes. Full thickness is painless, dry, leathery and does not blanch. Deep partial is less painful, with mottling and slow refill.

That is not right. The forearm is less painful, which points to deep partial, not full thickness.

That is not right. Classic Parkland gives crystalloid alone in the first 24 hours.

A 34-year-old man is brought in after a kitchen fire. He has burns over the head and neck, the whole front of the trunk and the perineum.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

That is not right. The head looks like the biggest part of this burn, so it is tempting to give it the larger figure.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the belief to replace: the adult head is not the big block of the chart. The legs and trunk are.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the small regions: a tiny region still counts, and the chart reserves a figure for it.

choices.label: I know both charts: skip to the final check

Now a 2-year-old with scalds over the whole head and both legs.
Which method should you use to estimate the TBSA?

Not sure, give me a hint

Same 2-year-old: the whole head and both whole legs are burnt.
Total TBSA on the child chart?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Do the head first, then one leg, then double the leg. Use the child figures for each, not the adult ones.
That is not right. Those are adult figures for both regions: the head as an adult's and the legs as adults'.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the belief to replace: the adult chart is not the default once the stem gives a child's age.

say.text: That is not right. The head looks correct, and then the leg feels right too, so the adult leg figure slipped in.
That mixes two models. Once the head follows the child chart, use the child rule for every region, legs included.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the mix: one age rule applies to every region, not a child head with adult legs.

Total each pair: arms, legs, and the trunk front plus back.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

That is not right. The head is a big region, so 18 feels like a head figure.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the smallest region: it takes the smallest figure on the chart.

A 40% burn can need several litres of fluid in the first day. Why does so much volume leave the circulation?

choices.label: The burn damages the heart, so it needs volume to restore output
Capillary leak drains plasma out of the circulation for hours
The wound is infected, and sepsis needs large volume to clear it
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the burn does to the blood vessels first, before any pump problem or infection.
Yes. Mediators released by the burn raise capillary permeability, so plasma leaks out. The leak is maximal in the first 8 to 12 hours and continues up to 24 hours.
That makes burn shock mainly hypovolaemic, and Ringer lactate is the fluid of choice.
That is not right. A fast pulse and low pressure make the heart look like the culprit, but myocardial depression is only an added factor in burn shock.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the main cause before the added factor. Ask what the volume is replacing.

say.text: That is not right. A very sick patient feels septic, but infection of the wound is not what drains the circulation in the first hours.

What is the 24-hour Ringer lactate volume?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

K1.text: Burns are assessed by depth, % total body surface area (TBSA), age and inhalation injury. Large burns cause burn shock from capillary leak, which is treated with calculated crystalloid (Ringer lactate) titrated to urine output. The Parkland formula and the rule of nines are the most-tested items.

K2.text: **Parkland (Baxter) formula**: 4 mL x body weight (kg) x %TBSA burned of **Ringer lactate** over 24 h; half in the first 8 h counted from the time of burn, half in the next 16 h.

K3.text: Maintenance fluid is added in children, and the formula is only a starting estimate to be titrated to urine output.

K4.text: **Rule of nines** (adult): head and neck 9, each upper limb 9, anterior trunk 18, posterior trunk 18, each lower limb 18, perineum 1.

K5.text: Child (infant) head is about 18% and each lower limb about 14%, so the adult rule of nines overestimates the legs and underestimates the head in children; the **Lund and Browder chart** corrects for age.

K6.text: Patient's palm including fingers is about **1% TBSA**, used for small or patchy burns.

K7.text: Urine output target: **0.5 mL/kg/h** in adults (30-50 mL/h) and **1 mL/kg/h** in children.

K8.text: Simple erythema (superficial/first-degree) is **not counted** in TBSA for resuscitation.

K9.text: Inhalation injury and carbon monoxide poisoning are the leading cause of early death at the scene; give **100% oxygen**.

K10.text: Circumferential full-thickness burns of the limb or chest need **escharotomy**.

K17.text: Local burn releases histamine, prostaglandins, oxygen free radicals and other mediators that raise capillary permeability; the leak is maximal in the first 8-12 h and continues up to 24 h.

K18.text: Large burns (above about 30% TBSA) cause systemic capillary leak even in uninjured tissue, with loss of plasma volume, haemoconcentration (rising haematocrit), hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.

K19.text: Burn shock is predominantly **hypovolaemic**, with added myocardial depression from circulating mediators.

K23.text: Superficial (first degree): epidermis only; red, painful, dry, blanches, no blisters; heals in about 7 days without scar.

K24.text: Superficial partial thickness (superficial second degree): blisters, moist, pink, very painful, blanches; heals in 2-3 weeks.

K25.text: Deep partial thickness (deep second degree): mottled red-white, less painful, sluggish capillary refill, may heal in more than 3 weeks with scarring and often needs grafting.

K26.text: Full thickness (third degree): white, brown or leathery, dry, **painless** (insensate), does not blanch; needs excision and grafting.

K28.text: The commonest error in assessment is underestimating depth, which declares itself over 48-72 h.

K29.text: Features of **inhalation injury**: burns in a closed space, singed nasal hair or eyebrows, facial burns, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, wheeze, soot in the oropharynx.

K30.text: **Carbon monoxide poisoning**: headache, confusion, cherry-red skin (late and unreliable); pulse oximetry reads falsely normal because it cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.

K31.text: Signs of inadequate resuscitation: tachycardia, low urine output, rising lactate and base deficit, rising haematocrit.

K32.text: Primary survey (ABCDE as in ATLS) comes first, with cervical spine protection if trauma is suspected; burn assessment is done in the secondary survey.

K33.text: **Carboxyhaemoglobin level** and arterial blood gas (SaO2 on co-oximetry, lactate, base deficit).

K34.text: **Fibreoptic bronchoscopy** is the best test to confirm inhalation injury (soot, oedema, erythema below the cords).

K35.text: Baseline: CBC, urea and electrolytes, glucose, creatinine, creatine kinase and urine myoglobin in electrical or deep burns, ECG in electrical burns, chest X-ray (often normal early).

K36.text: Estimate TBSA with the rule of nines, Lund and Browder chart or palm method; count only partial-thickness and full-thickness areas.

K38.text: Cover with clean cling film or dry sterile sheet; high-flow 100% oxygen if inhalation or CO exposure is suspected.

K39.text: **Early intubation** before oedema develops if there is stridor, hoarseness, deep facial or neck burns, extensive oropharyngeal soot or a falling level of consciousness.

K40.text: In CO poisoning, 100% oxygen reduces the COHb half-life from about 4-5 h on room air to about 1 h; hyperbaric oxygen reduces it further and is reserved for selected cases.

K41.text: Suspect cyanide poisoning (smoke from burning plastics) with unexplained lactic acidosis or shock; treat with **hydroxocobalamin**.

K43.text: **Parkland formula**: 4 mL x kg x %TBSA of Ringer lactate in 24 h; first half over the first 8 h from the time of injury (not time of arrival), second half over the next 16 h.

K44.text: Worked example: 70 kg adult, 40% TBSA gives 4 x 70 x 40 = 11,200 mL in 24 h; 5,600 mL in the first 8 h (700 mL/h) and 5,600 mL in the next 16 h (350 mL/h).

K45.text: Fluid already given before arrival is deducted from the first-8-hour volume, and the rate is **titrated hourly** to urine output rather than followed rigidly.

K46.text: The Parkland formula uses crystalloid only; **no colloid in the first 24 h** in the classic Parkland protocol, with colloid (albumin) considered after the capillary leak settles (about 8-24 h) or when requirements are very high.

K47.text: Current ATLS and ABA-type practice starts lower, at about 2 mL/kg/%TBSA/24 h in adults (3 mL in children), then adjusts to urine output, to limit "fluid creep".

K50.text: Other formulae: **Brooke** (1.5 mL crystalloid + 0.5 mL colloid /kg/%TBSA plus 2 L dextrose in 5% water), **Evans** (1 mL crystalloid + 1 mL colloid /kg/%TBSA plus 2 L dextrose), **modified Brooke** (2 mL Ringer lactate/kg/%TBSA, no colloid).

K51.text: **Monitoring**: urine output hourly with a catheter (0.5 mL/kg/h adult, 1 mL/kg/h child), heart rate, blood pressure, base deficit and lactate; if urine output is low, increase fluid by about 20-25%, and if high, reduce the rate.

K52.text: Over-resuscitation causes pulmonary oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome and compartment syndromes in limbs.

K53.text: **Electrical burns** and rhabdomyolysis: increase fluids to maintain urine output at about 1-1.5 mL/kg/h (higher target, about 75-100 mL/h in adults), with urine alkalinisation not routinely required if output is adequate.

K54.text: Ringer lactate is preferred over normal saline because large volumes of saline cause hyperchloraemic acidosis.

K56.text: **Escharotomy** for circumferential full-thickness limb burns (distal ischaemia, loss of pulses) and chest burns (restricted ventilation); incisions are along the midlateral and midaxial lines through eschar only, and can be done at the bedside without anaesthesia since full-thickness skin is insensate.

K57.text: Topical agents: **silver sulfadiazine** (broad spectrum, painless; causes transient leucopenia, avoided in sulfa allergy and on the face), **mafenide acetate** (penetrates eschar, good for ear cartilage; causes metabolic acidosis through carbonic anhydrase inhibition and is painful), **silver nitrate 0.5%** (stains black, causes hyponatraemia and hypochloraemia), **povidone iodine**.

K60.text: Stress ulcer prophylaxis for **Curling's ulcer** (acute gastroduodenal ulcer after major burns).

K65.text: Late: **burn wound sepsis** (Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic most common organism in later burn infection; Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci early), pneumonia, Curling's ulcer, hypermetabolism and malnutrition, venous thrombosis.

K66.text: Sepsis is the commonest cause of death after the first 48-72 h in patients who survive resuscitation.

K67.text: Scars: hypertrophic scars and **keloid**, contractures, and **Marjolin's ulcer** (squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic burn scar).

K68.text: Fluid of choice for burn resuscitation — Ringer lactate

K72.text: Investigation of choice for inhalation injury — Fibreoptic bronchoscopy

K74.text: Treatment of cyanide poisoning in smoke inhalation — Hydroxocobalamin

K75.text: Topical agent that penetrates eschar — Mafenide acetate

K76.text: Topical agent causing metabolic acidosis — Mafenide

K77.text: Topical agent causing leucopenia — Silver sulfadiazine

K78.text: Topical agent causing hyponatraemia, black stain — Silver nitrate

K80.text: Stress ulcer after burns — Curling's ulcer

K81.text: Hydrofluoric acid burn antidote — Calcium gluconate

K82.text: PYQs have expected the Parkland formula as 4 mL/kg/%TBSA with Ringer lactate, half in the first 8 h; current ATLS and ABA-style practice starts lower (about 2 mL/kg/%TBSA in adults) and titrates to urine output to avoid fluid creep. Always answer 4 mL unless the question says "modified" or "current".

K83.text: The 8 h is counted from the **time of burn**, not from arrival at hospital.

K85.text: Child head/legs: infant head 18%, leg 14% each; the adult rule of nines is the key's default unless the stem says child.

K86.text: Pulse oximetry is falsely normal in CO poisoning, a favoured trap.

K87.text: Colloid: classic Parkland gives none in the first 24 h; Evans and Brooke include colloid.

shaky.text: TBSA estimation is shaky. Re-derive the adult total (9, 9, 9, 18, 18, 18, 18, 1 makes 100) and ask age first, because infant head and leg figures are 18 and 14. Redo the TBSA card.

gap.text: TBSA estimation is a gap. Two things are going wrong: region figures get swapped, and the adult rule of nines is used on a child. Check the 100 total, make age your first question, and review the TBSA card.

secure.text: Parkland arithmetic is secure. You read the qualifier word, started the clock at the burn, and deducted fluid already given before setting the rate.

shaky.text: Parkland arithmetic is shaky. Run it in order: find time of burn, set the first half over 8 h from then, subtract fluid already given, divide by the time left. Note the exam key is 4 mL, while current practice starts near 2 mL. Redo the Parkland card.

gap.text: Parkland arithmetic is a gap. Common wrong models: the clock starts at arrival, the half lands on the wrong quantity, or pre-hospital fluid is ignored. Practise total, half, divide by hours remaining, minus fluid given. Review the Parkland card, then retry the worked example.

secure.text: Titration is secure. You treated the formula as a starting estimate, raised fluid for low urine and lowered it for high, and picked the right target for age and setting.

shaky.text: Titration is shaky. Keep the direction and the target in mind: low urine means raise the rate by about 20-25%, high urine means lower it, and the target changes for children and electrical injury. Redo the titration card.

gap.text: Titration is a gap. The wrong model is a prescription to deliver, or urine output read as a demand signal. Urine is a perfusion signal: low raises the rate, high lowers it, and children and electrical burns need higher targets. Review the titration and urine-target cards.

secure.text: Topical agent pairing is secure. You matched each agent to its own property and side effect.

shaky.text: Topical agent pairing is shaky. Rebuild a four-row table: mafenide penetrates eschar and causes acidosis, silver sulfadiazine is painless with transient leucopenia, silver nitrate stains and lowers sodium. Redo the topical card.

gap.text: Topical agent pairing is a gap. Side effects are being swapped between agents, and silver sulfadiazine becomes the default for everything. Learn the four-row table, starting with mafenide for eschar and ear cartilage. Review the topical card.

secure.text: Curling and Marjolin are secure. You placed Curling's ulcer in the gut early after a burn and Marjolin's ulcer in an old scar as squamous cell carcinoma.

shaky.text: Curling and Marjolin are shaky. Sort them by site and timing, not by the shared word burn: Curling is gut, early, stress ulcer; Marjolin is scar, late, squamous cell carcinoma. Redo the ulcer card.

gap.text: Curling and Marjolin are a gap. The two eponyms are being swapped because both say burn. Pair gut with early and scar with late. Review the ulcer card, then say each aloud with its organ and timing.

secure.text: Escharotomy is secure. You asked whether the eschar is constricting, and kept both qualifiers: full thickness and circumferential with compromise.

shaky.text: Escharotomy is shaky. Both qualifiers must hold: full-thickness eschar that is inelastic, and circumferential constriction with falling pulses or restricted chest movement. Redo the escharotomy card.

gap.text: Escharotomy is a gap. The wrong model is deep burn means cut. Partial-thickness skin stays elastic. Release is for circumferential full-thickness burns with distal ischaemia or restricted ventilation. Review the escharotomy card.

avoided.text: You separated the exam key from current practice.

fell_recovered.text: You changed your mind once you saw the qualifier. The 4 mL reflex can return under exam pressure, so read the stem for words like current or modified before you compute.

fell_open.text: Model: 4 mL/kg is the only fluid formula. You may have corrected it on the spot, but it has not been shown to hold. Exam key is 4 mL; current practice starts near 2 mL and titrates. Meet it again on a fresh question with the Parkland review card.

avoided.text: You started the clock at the burn, not at arrival.

fell_recovered.text: You moved the clock to the time of burn. Under pressure, now feels like time zero, so check the burn time first.

fell_open.text: Model: the 8 h starts when the patient reaches the team. You may have fixed it on the spot, but not on a later question. Capillary leak begins at injury, so the first half runs from the burn. Meet it again on the Parkland review card.

avoided.text: Your total, half and divide steps are secure.

fell_recovered.text: You corrected where the half goes. Under pressure the phrase half in 8 hours can slip onto the wrong quantity, so rebuild it: total, half, divide by hours.

fell_open.text: Model: half in 8 h is a phrase, not a calculation. You may have corrected it on the spot, but it was not tested again. Anchor it: 11,200 total, 5,600 first half, 700 mL/h, then 350 mL/h. Retry it on the Parkland review card.

avoided.text: You credited fluid already given before arrival.

fell_recovered.text: You started deducting pre-hospital fluid. Under pressure the formula number feels complete, so ask what has already been given.

fell_open.text: Model: the formula is a standalone prescription. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Subtract fluid already given from the first-half volume, then spread the rest over the time left. Meet it again on the Parkland review card.

avoided.text: You checked age before reaching for the adult chart.

fell_recovered.text: You switched to child figures after the slip. The adult chart is a strong default under pressure, so ask age first.

fell_open.text: Model: the rule of nines works for everyone. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Infant head is 18 and each leg 14, so use Lund and Browder in children. Meet it again with the TBSA review card.

avoided.text: You kept formula and fluid pairs distinct.

fell_recovered.text: You separated Parkland from the colloid formulae. Under pressure Evans, Brooke and Parkland blur, so recall the pairs before choosing.

fell_open.text: Model: Parkland, Brooke and Evans all mix colloid and crystalloid. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Classic Parkland is Ringer lactate alone; Evans and Brooke add colloid. Rebuild the pairs table with the fluid review card.

avoided.text: You held that bronchoscopy, not X-ray or ABG, confirms inhalation injury.

fell_recovered.text: You moved from the familiar test to the confirming one. Under pressure a normal X-ray tempts reassurance, so keep the ladder in mind.

fell_open.text: Model: the routine test is the confirming test. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. X-ray is often normal early, ABG shows gas exchange, and only bronchoscopy shows the airway. Meet it again with the inhalation review card.

avoided.text: You did not trust a normal oximeter reading in smoke exposure.

fell_recovered.text: You learned why oximetry misleads. It is a favoured exam trap and a normal number is reassuring under pressure, so ask whether carbon monoxide is possible first.

fell_open.text: Model: a normal SpO2 shows haemoglobin is carrying oxygen. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Oximetry cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so send co-oximetry. Meet it again with the inhalation review card.

avoided.text: You kept Curling and Marjolin apart.

fell_recovered.text: You sorted the two ulcers after a swap. Both say burn, so pair each with its organ and timing again when you are rushed.

fell_open.text: Model: both eponyms mean a burn ulcer. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Curling is gut and early; Marjolin is scar and late, squamous cell carcinoma. Meet it again with the ulcer review card.

avoided.text: You treated the formula as a starting estimate.

fell_recovered.text: You moved from delivering the formula to titrating it. Under pressure the first calculated number feels like the order, so check urine output hourly.

fell_open.text: Model: the formula is a prescription to deliver. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Urine output is the feedback: low raises the rate, high lowers it. This is the commonest management error. Meet it again with the titration review card.

avoided.text: Your titration direction was right.

fell_recovered.text: You reversed your direction after the slip. Under pressure high output can feel like a signal for more fluid, so ask what it says about perfusion.

fell_open.text: Model: urine output is a demand signal. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. It measures perfusion: low means raise by about 20-25%, high means lower, and excess risks pulmonary oedema. Meet it again with the titration review card.

avoided.text: You separated reduced pain from absent pain.

fell_recovered.text: You learned to use blanching and sensation, not pain alone. Under pressure less painful can still pull you towards full thickness.

fell_open.text: Model: pain falls in a straight line with depth. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Deep partial is less painful with sluggish refill; full thickness is leathery, non-blanching and insensate. Meet it again with the depth review card.

avoided.text: You matched the urine target to the patient.

fell_recovered.text: You linked the target to child and electrical settings. Under pressure the adult figure is the first one retrieved, so check age and injury type.

fell_open.text: Model: one urine target fits everyone. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Adult is 0.5 mL/kg/h, child 1 mL/kg/h, and electrical burns with myoglobinuria about 1-1.5 mL/kg/h. Meet it again with the urine-target review card.

avoided.text: You kept the region figures straight.

fell_recovered.text: You fixed the swapped figures. Under pressure 9 and 18 get transposed, so recheck the total of 100.

fell_open.text: Model: remembering that there are 9s and 18s is enough. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Re-derive: 9, 9, 9, 18, 18, 18, 18, 1 makes 100, with perineum at 1. Meet it again with the TBSA review card.

avoided.text: You asked whether the eschar was constricting.

fell_recovered.text: You added both escharotomy qualifiers after the slip. Under pressure deep reads as cut, so ask about full thickness and compromise.

fell_open.text: Model: any deep burn needs escharotomy. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. It needs circumferential full-thickness eschar with distal ischaemia or restricted ventilation. Meet it again with the escharotomy review card.

avoided.text: You paired topical agents with the right property.

fell_recovered.text: You corrected the agent pairs. Under pressure silver sulfadiazine becomes the default, so recall each agent's own property.

fell_open.text: Model: topical agents are one bag of facts, with silver sulfadiazine as the default. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Mafenide penetrates eschar and causes acidosis; silver sulfadiazine causes leucopenia. Meet it again with the topical review card.

avoided.text: You kept the carbon monoxide and cyanide treatments apart.

fell_recovered.text: You separated the two poisons. Under pressure one fire means one oxygen treatment, so name each by mechanism.

fell_open.text: Model: smoke poisoning is one entity with one oxygen treatment. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Carbon monoxide gets 100% oxygen; cyanide, suspected with unexplained lactic acidosis, gets hydroxocobalamin. Meet it again with the antidote review card.

avoided.text: You put the primary survey before the numbers.

fell_recovered.text: You reordered the plan to put the airway first. Under pressure the burn-specific calculation feels like the real work, so run ABCDE first.

fell_open.text: Model: burn numbers come before ABCDE. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Airway can close within hours while the sums can wait minutes; TBSA belongs to the secondary survey. Meet it again with the airway review card.

avoided.text: You acted on airway red flags early.

fell_recovered.text: You changed to acting before the oedema. A comfortable patient is the temptation under pressure, so react to soot and hoarseness, not to current comfort.

fell_open.text: Model: wait for stridor, then intubate. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Swelling peaks after fluids start and can make later intubation impossible. Meet it again with the airway review card.

avoided.text: You named burn shock as hypovolaemic.

fell_recovered.text: You moved to plasma loss as the cause. Under pressure septic or cardiogenic look-alikes pull, so start from the rising haematocrit.

fell_open.text: Model: the most visible feature names the shock. You may have corrected it on the spot, but not on a later question. Burn shock is mainly hypovolaemic from capillary leak, with haematocrit rising and urine falling. Meet it again with the shock review card.

E1.text: You tend to name a condition from its most visible feature rather than its cause or discriminator, in depth grading and shock type. Before answering, ask what separates this from its look-alike: blanching and sensation for depth, haematocrit and plasma loss for shock.

E3.text: You tend to reverse the direction of a response to a signal. Before adjusting, name what the signal measures, such as perfusion for urine output, then decide which way to move.

E4.text: You tend to treat a starting estimate as a fixed order. Look for words like starting, estimate and titrate, and ask what feedback should change the plan.

E5.text: You tend to answer with the memorised exam figure without reading qualifiers. Check the stem for words such as current or modified before choosing between 4 mL and 2 mL.

E6.text: You tend to mix up figures that you hold as a list: halves, rates, urine targets and region values. Anchor each number to the quantity it describes, and check totals such as 100 for TBSA.

E7.text: You tend to apply a default rule across patients without checking the qualifier: adult chart for children, deep burn for escharotomy. Make the qualifier your first check: age, thickness, constriction.

E8.text: You tend to stop at the familiar test and trust it, such as X-ray or oximetry. Ask what each test actually measures before you let it reassure you.

E9.text: You tend to get the order or the clock wrong: arrival for burn time, calculation for airway, waiting for action. Write the steps in sequence and ask what first, and why.

E10.text: You tend to swap pairs held as separate facts: formulae and fluids, agents and side effects, antidotes and poisons, eponyms. Use a small table or a one-line contrast for each set rather than recalling items alone.

overconfident.text: Twice or more you tapped Sure on an answer that was wrong. Those confident errors are the ones to fix first, so their cards are listed first. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier in the stem that makes you certain.

underconfident.text: Several times you tapped Guessing and were right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Next time, say the reason to yourself before choosing; if you can, tap Sure.

calibrated.text: Your Sure and Guessing taps tracked your answers well. That is useful: you know when to trust yourself and when to check. Keep using the taps honestly, since the review cards rely on them.

hints_heavy.text: You asked for hints or explanations often. That is a sound strategy while learning, and it shows what the module can teach. Cold questions show what holds without help, so on your next pass answer first and ask afterwards.

hints_none.text: You did not ask for hints, so each slip was an unaided attempt. Next time, when two options feel close, open a hint before committing. It is cheaper to ask than to rehearse the wrong model.

hinted_only.text: On some objectives you were right only after opening a hint. That is real progress, but it does not yet show you can do it alone. Those objectives are in the review cards; try them cold before the module.

fast_lane.text: You skipped part of a lesson. The skipped lesson's content is untested for you, so do its review cards soon, answering cold. If they come easily, the skip was reasonable; if not, rerun that segment.

gap.text: Work the review cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky objectives. Do one card per objective, say the answer aloud, then check. Rerun the module after a day and aim to change your first answers, not only your retries.

clear.text: No objective needs rescue. Keep the review cards on their spaced schedule at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days. When you see a burn fluid question, still read the stem for age, timing and qualifier words before computing.
